title: The Serial Scaling Hypothesis
claim: Some problems decompose into many independent parts solvable in parallel, while others have interdependent steps that force sequential computation.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, stacked easy grids vs one hard grid with red dependency graph
description: Two side-by-side panels show Sudoku grids. On the left, a stack of several mostly filled Sudoku boards is drawn, with the front board showing four red circles on blank cells. These cells can be filled independently, which suggests many easy puzzles solved in parallel. On the right, a single sparse Sudoku grid has a few given digits and four red circles on blank cells. Thick red lines join the circles in a star shape around a central circle, showing that the blanks depend on each other. The red circles and lines draw the eye first. The contrast between a dense stack of easy boards and one sparse board with a dependency graph carries the argument. There are no arrows or text labels.
caption: (Left) Many easy Sudoku puzzles, where the circled blanks can be filled independently in parallel. (Right) A hard Sudoku with the same total compute, but the circled blanks are interdependent, requiring sequential reasoning.
abstract: While machine learning has advanced through massive parallelization, we identify a critical blind spot: some problems are fundamentally sequential. These "inherently serial" problems-from mathematical reasoning to physical simulations to sequential decision-making-require sequentially dependent computational steps that cannot be efficiently parallelized. We formalize this distinction in complexity theory, and demonstrate that current parallel-centric architectures face fundamental limitations on such tasks. Then, we show for first time that diffusion models despite their sequential nature are incapable of solving inherently serial problems. We argue that recognizing the serial nature of computation holds profound implications on machine learning, model design, and hardware development.
